I am a pilot. That's a good story but very unlikely to be entirely accurate. Once, when I was 6'3" and 125lbs, I've been asked to move on a commercial flight for weight and balance. Have also been asked to sit right seat on a private flight for W&B. What you're failing to account for is fuel load and cargo. If they were light on fuel and cargo, they likely want everyone moved forward, especially since weight and balance (W&B) will continue to shift as fuel is burned off while in flight.

Some smaller aircraft actually have kick stands near the aft to prevent the aircraft from tipping back during cargo or passenger loading. It balances back out as passengers are seated and/or the aircraft is fueled. Accordingly, they want everyone loaded as required for best W&B reflective of the entire flight profile.

Many aircraft accidents occur from improper W&B. As a side note, the FAA's standard passenger weight is 170lbs. Few Americans qualify any more. A/V media techie here.

The cheap-ass way is to get an affordable projector ($100-$300 price range, should be mountable) and a background (e.g. a white sheet) to project on. Super easy to transport and set up, simple to get your video source working (just plug in HDMI in, select right source, done) but cheap projectors usually only have 1500-2200 lumen and look like shit in anything but perfect lighting conditions. Also the brightness becomes worse over time as the bulb slowly craps out.

A set of decent LCDs that covers about the same area as a cheap projector will be significantly more expensive ($1500-$3000, more if you buy them debezelled) and it's a proper pain in the ass to find suitable VESA mounts. Transport and setup is a challenge. Getting your video source to work properly gets exponentially more difficult with every LCD you add to the array - using something like a laptop with a dongle to feed video becomes unfeasible after more than ~3 monitors, so you'll likely have to look into getting some video management hardware to mix the feed you're sending to the LCDs. Cable management is a bitch. But, as you said, LCDs look better in most conditions.

Alternatively you could go for a full-on stage projector (hi-lumen, lots of inputs, wide FoV) and a nice big screen, which will likely give you even better quality over LCDs, but those are expensive as hell. Entry-level is around $6000.

In my experience Murphy's law very much applies to spare parts - when you buy a ton of replaceables up front your kit runs like clockwork for all eternity, and when you only buy enough to cover for one major fuck-up it happens immediately and the manufacturer declares bankruptcy two weeks after.

I'd say if you're buying from one of the giants (Sony, Panasonic, Optoma) you can be reasonably sure that spares will be around when you need them, but I'd still stockpile at least enough bulbs for 3000h-5000h. How quickly you'll wear them down depends on your usage patterns - most of the mid-range projectors I had lasted for 3-5 years of light usage before dimming became noticeable. Honestly can't tell you much about the lifespan of high-end stage projectors since I haven't had the opportunity to work with kit like that, but I'd expect bulb lifespan to linearly decrease the more brightness you have.

If you expect rough handling & transport I'd also invest in one additional lens, those things are rather fragile and I've had issues with dust/smears/scratches in the past. I think most projector lenses nowadays are not user-serviceable, so a "some idiot spilled his beer so spectacularly he somehow managed to hit the lens"-type situation can lead to a total loss.

100k is a nice budget. Two good projectors with spares and a decent screen seems doable with ~30k or less, but don't quote me on that. In my personal experience the most annoying and time-consuming part is finding mounts/racks that do what you want them to and don't come crashing down when someone as much as farts at them.
